621.s: Duhé praises E.T. Thomas as a high-register trumpeter trained under Professor O'Jay in Crowley.
621.q: High C's. Somebody said he was trained up in Boston or so. No, sir, he was trained under Professor O'Jay right in Crowley. Oh, right in Crowley. Yeah, the man there, Professor O'Jay, had five years conservatory playing in all foreign countries. He played from a bazoon up. And you'd whistle a tune…

49.t: Manuel Mineta, the High Society variation and Hardy
49.s: He says the High Society cornet variation originated with Manuel Mineta, who taught it to Hardy, and that Red Allen got it by copying Hardy's version.
49.ch: Emmett Hardy and the river towns
49.q: The, the, the old colored fellow over here. He studied from Manuel Mineta. And, uh, this thing on high society. You know, the, the, da, The baronet variation. Well, that's, that belongs to Manuel Mineta. Manuel Mineta, uh, created that, or whatever you want to call it. He was the first one to play…

484.t: Manuel Moneta, Turk Rene's range and Al Hirt
484.s: The interviewer took lessons from Manuel Moneta, who taught Hardy and Rene. Brownlee describes Rene's reading and high notes, and compares Al Hirt's range.
484.ch: Depression years and New Orleans trumpeters
484.q: Well, Turk René, Turk René in those days, a lot of the, a lot of the musicians didn't bother about reading. Mm-hmm. But, uh, Turk always read. He could always read his music. And, uh, I hear him going up for screaming notes, and I've heard Turk make some of the clearest, finest high notes I've…

830.t: Little George's playing style, lip and the WPA band
830.s: Charlotte describes her brother's held notes, range, Dixieland and reading ability, and the last time his mother heard him with the WPA band.
830.q: And did he play that solo? He was living right there on Russia. Yeah. He was one of trumpet players that you could open a book and knock it off. And yeah. I don't know it was on that page. Yeah. I don't know it was on that page. I don't know.

739.t: Playing along with Chet Baker, Miles and Maynard Ferguson
739.s: As a young trumpeter he played along with records; Chet Baker was playable, Dizzy and Maynard were out of reach.
739.q: Maybe through Chet Baker. Because when I really started to get interested in jazz I would have probably been eighth or ninth grade, and I was trying to find records of trumpet players even though I didn’t — maybe didn’t know who they were — to play along with, or to try to play with. And so I had…

364.t: Bobby Hackett as teacher and musician
364.s: Hackett's harmonic knowledge and teaching; upcoming tribute concert.
364.q: Yes he did that’s very true. He’s one of the few in those days that did, of the horn players. Horn players, most of them played by instinct, by ear, by hearing. But Bobby knew his changes. And like some of these other guys just played — I mean they did just as well in a lot of cases. But Bobby’s…

17.s: Clark kept a mouthpiece in his pocket.
17.ch: Rhythm Club memories and playing technique
17.q: Trumpet player. Later on in years, because he hadn't played in a while, he was, Ray Robinson, the fighter, he was Ray Robinson's manager, and June Clark was a very dear friend of all the guys, all the musicians, and he was a good trumpet player. Something I think he was, he had tuberculosis, the…

28.t: Fats Navarro's big sound and Freddie Hubbard
28.s: Navarro had a big sound from his mouthpiece and training, and Butler says Freddie Hubbard plays everyone's style, advising to perfect what one is.
28.q: Now, he plays everybody. See. He played that first part, and all them parts, and don't turn him loose because he's a demon. So, there you are.

169.t: Fats Navarro in the trumpet section: McGhee's playing and high C
169.s: McGhee sits between Caypart and Fats, plays 'McGhee Special', and Fats asks how he does it; he can't play above high C.
169.ch: Hampton, Andy Kirk and Charlie Barnet
169.q: : Yeah, Arthur Caypart. I don't know whether you know him or not. Light-skinned colored fellow that played decent trumpet; nothing to brag about, but a decent trumpet. And me. So the only place I could sit would be between Caypart and Fats, because I wanted to hear Fats myself. Boy, he was so…

124.t: Cat Anderson's high C's and his teacher
124.s: McRae says Cat Anderson's non-pressure study with a teacher let him hit five C's, which no one on television bands could match.
124.ch: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
124.q: Just like the trumpet -- the teacher that Cat Anderson studied with. The guy told Cat Anderson, "You stay with me, I'll make you the greatest trumpet player in the business." And he did.
